query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation in the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy during high-temperature exposure is driven by the selective oxidation of titanium and chromium. In oxidizing environments, the rapid formation of a duplex oxide scale occurs with an inner, porous, Ti-rich oxide and a thin, less protective Cr-rich outer layer. In reducing environments, incomplete oxidation leads to sub-stoichiometric or discontinuous oxide scales that generate internal stresses and microcracking at grain boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneously microstructured, single-phase FCC matrix produced via additive manufacturing that shows high strength and fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Expose samples at elevated temperatures (e.g., 800–1200 °C) in controlled gas environments that are either oxidizing (e.g., air or O2-rich) or reducing (e.g., H2-containing mixtures).
generation.conditions: Testing conducted between 800 °C and 1200 °C for times ranging from 100 to 1000 hours under well‐controlled gas atmospheres to isolate the effects of oxidation dynamics versus reduction-induced changes.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of a duplex oxide scale composed of a porous, Ti-rich inner layer and a thin, Cr-rich outer layer, along with induced microcracks along the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Selective oxidation kinetics cause Ti to oxidize rapidly, forming a porous inner oxide that fails to provide comprehensive protection, while Cr oxidizes more slowly, yielding a thinner outer layer that cannot fully compensate. In reducing atmospheres, the incomplete oxide formation leads to sub-stoichiometric scales and greater internal stress, which in turn promote microstructural degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, a moderately protective but increasingly thick oxide scale develops, resulting in gradual degradation. In reducing conditions, the formation of discontinuous or sub-stoichiometric oxides leads to enhanced microcracking and void formation at grain boundaries, thereby accelerating degradation relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The as-fabricated, single-phase FCC alloy with a uniform microstructure, high strength, and good fatigue performance prior to any elevated-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be most relevant for exposures at 800–1200 °C for up to 1000 hours in atmospheres with typical oxidizing (air, O2-rich) or reducing (H2-containing) conditions; outside these boundaries, different degradation mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the selective oxidation of Ti and Cr is supported by analogous studies in complex alloys, the precise oxide scale thickness, porosity, and the stress state induced by sub-stoichiometric oxides remain to be quantified. The relative contributions of Ti versus Cr oxidation kinetics under different gas atmospheres require further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of identical additively manufactured alloy samples and subject them to identical thermal profiles (800–1200 °C) in two distinct environments: one oxidizing and one reducing. Perform time-resolved surface and cross-sectional analyses using SEM, TEM, and XPS/EDS to characterize the oxide scale morphology, composition, and microcrack development along grain boundaries. Additionally, conduct mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and fatigue testing) both before and after exposure to determine the extent of degradation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and compositional gradients (Ti-rich vs Cr-rich layers)
Degree of porosity and evidence of microcracks at grain boundaries
Changes in mechanical properties such as ultimate tensile strength and fatigue life
Kinetics of oxidation by tracking mass gain or loss over time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If identical or non-discriminatory oxide scales are observed in both oxidizing and reducing conditions—i.e., if there is no evidence of a duplex oxide structure or differential microcracking—and if mechanical properties degrade at similar rates irrespective of the gas environment, then the hypothesis (that selective oxidation of Ti and Cr governs degradation via duplex oxide formation and induced microcracking) is falsified.
